Ebenezer Scrooge. The miser and misanthrope in A Christmas Carol whose life of callous indifference is transformed by supernatural visitation on Christmas Eve, moving him toward genuine charity and human connection. A London moneylender obsessed with profit and contemptuous of the poor, he utters the phrase "If they would rather die, they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population." On Christmas Eve, he is haunted by the ghosts of Christmas Past, Present, and Yet to Come, forced to witness the consequences of his greed and the fate awaiting him if he remains unchanged. He is particularly moved by the vision of Tiny Tim's death and the revelation that his actions and indifference contribute to the suffering of innocents. Awakening on Christmas morning transformed, he becomes a second father to Tiny Tim and raises the wages of his clerk Bob Cratchit. His redemption arc from denial to acceptance to transformation has become the archetypal conversion narrative in English literature. His phrase "Bah, humbug" becomes iconic shorthand for commercial cynicism, and his story represents Dickens' belief in the possibility of moral redemption through confrontation with consequence and the demands of compassion.
